Water Research.title: Reactive nitrogen intermediate regulation couples sulfur-driven denitrification with antibiotic transformation.
Water Research.abstract: The widespread presence of antibiotics in aquatic environments underscores a persistent challenge for conventional wastewater treatment systems, which are primarily designed to remove nutrients and readily biodegradable organic matter. Free nitrous acid (FNA), a transient reactive nitrogen intermediate capable of transforming antibiotics, remains difficult to regulate under engineered conditions. Here, we demonstrate that sulfur-driven autotrophic denitrification (SAD) provides a biological route to regulate FNA concentration through the coupled effects of microbial nitrite accumulation and sulfur oxidation-associated acidification. Functional differentiation in nitrate and nitrite reduction pathways among sulfur-autotrophic denitrifiers was associated with distinct nitrite accumulation and FNA dynamics. Sulfamethoxazole (SMX) transformation kinetics were strongly correlated with FNA concentrations across contrasting microbial, pH, and oxygen conditions. Time-resolved transformation products revealed sequential SMX conversion, and theoretical calculations supported the relative energetic favorability of the proposed FNA-induced transformation routes. 13C tracing provided direct evidence for partial mineralization of SMX-derived carbon. FNA-mediated transformation extended to structurally distinct antibiotics, including sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones, and tetracyclines. During 270 days of operation in S0-based treatment wetlands receiving nitrified effluent from a recirculating aquaculture system, the enrichment of sulfur-autotrophic denitrifiers was associated with increased FNA concentrations and enhanced SMX attenuation while maintaining stable nitrate removal. Mild pH regulation from 7.5 to 6.5 further increased FNA levels and more than doubled SMX removal without compromising nitrate removal. These findings establish SAD as a biological route for regulating reactive nitrogen intermediates, linking nitrogen cycling with antibiotic transformation and extending the functional scope of autotrophic denitrification beyond nutrient removal.

Water Research.title: Intensity-dependent reversal of magnetic field effects on biofilm-associated fouling in reclaimed water distribution systems.
Water Research.abstract: Magnetic field (MF) treatment has been proposed as a non-chemical strategy for fouling control in reclaimed-water distribution systems, yet previous studies have reported inconsistent outcomes. Whether these contrasting effects arise from differences in field intensity remains unclear. Here, pilot-scale reclaimed-water distribution systems were operated for 800 h under six MF intensities (0, 10, 30, 100, 300, and 600 mT) to determine how field intensity regulates fouling accumulation and biofilm development. Fouling responses reversed across the intensity gradient. Compared with the untreated control, 10 and 30 mT increased total fouling accumulation by 12.1-13.4% and 24.2-26.7%, respectively, whereas 100, 300, and 600 mT reduced it by 4.5-6.1%, 26.8-27.3%, and 41.9-42.5%, respectively. These changes were accompanied by intensity-dependent microbial physiological responses. Lower-intensity MFs (10-30 mT) induced a moderate increase in ROS-associated fluorescence together with enhanced antioxidant responses, and were associated with sustained cellular activity, greater EPS production, and denser biofilm-associated deposits. Higher-intensity MFs (100-600 mT) produced a much greater ROS-associated fluorescence signal, accompanied by impaired antioxidant defenses, intensified lipid peroxidation, reduced cellular activity, lower EPS production, and more fragmented fouling structures. Metatranscriptomic analysis further revealed clear functional differentiation in fouling communities, with lower-intensity MFs enriching pathways related to colonization, quorum sensing, carbon metabolism, ABC transport, antioxidant defense, and EPS-associated secretion, whereas higher-intensity MFs were associated with stress-related colonization responses, oxidative-stress-associated energy metabolism, and altered EPS/transport-associated functions. Overall, the results support an intensity-dependent reversal in the magnetic-field response within the tested range, with lower-intensity treatments associated with adaptive antioxidant regulation and higher-intensity treatments associated with oxidative damage. These findings help explain the inconsistent effects previously reported for MF treatment and highlight the importance of field-intensity optimization for reliable fouling control in reclaimed-water distribution systems.

Water Research.title: In-situ conversion of pollutants into catalysts: revealing high-valent bimetallic synergy for self-catalytic decomplexation of heavy-metal complexes.
Water Research.abstract: The decomplexation of heavy-metal complexes by advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) remains challenging due to stable metal-ligand coordination and energy-intensive operation. The ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) pathway is promising but remains constrained by stringent triggering conditions, such as strong alkalinity or UV irradiation. In real wastewater, heavy metals rarely exist alone; Co, Cu, Ni, and other metals coexist, creating both a challenge and an overlooked resource. Herein, using NTA-Ni as a model pollutant, we demonstrate that these coexisting metals can be exploited as in-situ co-catalysts, transforming metal pollutants from passive targets into active catalytic regulators. Trace Co(II) (10 μM) markedly enhances PMS activation, enabling a self-catalytic Co/Ni bimetallic-center strategy that achieves near-complete NTA-Ni decomplexation (98.9%) within 10 min at mild pH using only 1.0 mM PMS, a sixfold reduction in oxidant dosage relative to conventional AOPs. Mechanistic studies reveal that Ni/Co coupling reorganizes the coordination environment and accelerates interfacial electron transfer, redirecting PMS activation from a Ni‑centered to a thermodynamically favored Co‑centered pathway. This shift generates Co(IV)-dominated intermediates and promotes Ni(III) accumulation, which together trigger sulfate‑assisted coordination‑sphere reconstruction and destabilize the NTA-Ni framework. The strategy is effective for multiple complexed heavy metals, including Ni, Cu, Pb, Mn, and Cd, and remains robust in natural water matrices and real electroplating wastewaters, achieving >94% decomplexation efficiency and stable continuous-flow treatment. This work presents a cost-effective self-catalytic route that converts coexisting heavy metals into functional catalytic participants, offering a resource-utilization paradigm for complex industrial wastewater treatment.

Water Research.title: Dynamic interfacial charge buffering in single-atom nano-islands: breaking the activity-stability trade-off in catalytic ozonation.
Water Research.abstract: Heterogeneous catalytic ozonation is a promising process for removing refractory organic contaminants from wastewater. However, achieving high catalytic activity while maintaining stable performance under complex aqueous conditions remains a critical challenge. Here, we develop a Mn single-atom nano-island catalyst featuring dynamic interfacial charge buffering to overcome the activity-stability trade-off in water purification. The nano-island catalyst based on the CeO2 substrate (MnSA/FLP-CeO2) achieved efficient and robust removal of diverse organic contaminants in multiple water matrices, including secondary effluent of pharmaceutical wastewater. It exhibited markedly enhanced catalytic performance, with a 3.8-fold enhancement in normalized reaction kinetics compared with conventional CeO2, while maintaining stable contaminant removal over a broad pH from 3 to 11 with minimal Mn leaching. Mechanism investigations revealed that the small CeO2 nanoparticle islands stabilize atomically dispersed Mn sites and create asymmetric interfacial Mn-O-Ce sites, where Mn 3d-O 2p-Ce 4f orbital coupling facilitates interfacial charge redistribution and promotes the formation of critical intermediates *OO to generate ·OH. Meanwhile, the hydroxyl-rich bulk CeO2 sea buffers proton fluctuations to stabilize the local reaction microenvironment. Consequently, this nano-island catalyst occupied a previously unattained region of activity (mass activity) versus stability (pH robustness) among reported metal oxide and single-atom catalysts. This work provides a promising strategy for designing highly active and durable catalysts for sustainable water purification.

Water Research.title: Divergent time-lagged effects of aquatic vegetation types on organic pollution: 25 years of satellite-based retrieval in a large shallow lake.
Water Research.abstract: Organic pollution poses a persistent threat to large shallow lakes. Its responses to ecological restoration are often temporally delayed rather than instantaneous, which can obscure the timing of restoration effects and reduce the reliability of short-term assessments. Aquatic vegetation and algal blooms (AB) play important roles in organic pollution dynamics, but different aquatic components, such as floating and emergent aquatic vegetation (FEAV), submerged aquatic vegetation (SAV) and AB, exert distinct time-lagged correlations with chemical oxygen demand (COD) due to differences in biomass turnover and environmental conditions. However, the lag times, driving mechanisms, and predictive relevance of these component-specific effects remain poorly quantified. Here, we reconstructed half-yearly spatial datasets of four aquatic components (FEAV, SAV, AB, open water (OW)) and COD in Nansi Lake from 2000 to 2024, using 437 Landsat images, 35,798 COD monitoring records, field samples, UAV imagery, and multi-source environmental factors. Pixel-scale cross-correlation analysis was used to identify lagged effects of aquatic components on COD. Distinct aquatic components showed divergent lag structures. AB and OW were dominated by rapid responses of 0-0.5 years, FEAV showed intermediate lags of 1-1.5 years, and SAV exhibited longer lags of 2-2.5 years. These dominant lags represent the time offsets at which the correlations between component changes and COD are strongest, characterizing long-term temporal associations and highlighting the importance of accounting for antecedent aquatic conditions. These lagged relationships varied across sub-lakes, offshore gradients, and environmental backgrounds. SAV lags were mainly constrained by topographic and thermal conditions, whereas FEAV lags were more closely linked to water-surface fluctuations, vegetation-algal interactions, atmospheric disturbances, and local topographic conditions. To validate the ecological realism of these identified delays, the lag features were integrated into predictive models for COD retrieval. Incorporating these vegetation-leading lag features substantially improved COD prediction performance, with R² increasing from 0.35 to 0.51 and concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) increasing from 0.56 to 0.68, while RMSE and MAE decreased from 0.71 and 0.54 mg/L to 0.61 and 0.47 mg/L, respectively. These findings demonstrate that time-lagged associations between aquatic components and COD are ecologically meaningful and can improve the detection of delayed restoration signals, supporting more robust long-term organic pollution mitigation and adaptive management in large shallow lakes.

eLife.title: ATP8B1–TMEM30B flippase activity maintains stereocilia lipid asymmetry required for hearing
eLife.abstract: Sensory hair cells convert sound-induced vibrations into electrical signals through a process called mechano-electrical transduction (MET). While the protein components of the MET complex are well studied, increasing evidence indicates that MET channel properties are significantly modulated by the surrounding lipid bilayer. The asymmetric distribution of membrane lipids between the inner and outer membrane leaflets is well established to shape membrane mechanics. The recent discovery that the core MET components TMC1 and TMC2 also act as lipid scramblases suggests a direct role for membrane lipid asymmetry in the dynamic shaping of auditory transduction. Because scramblase activity of TMC1/2 disrupts lipid asymmetry, we hypothesized that an opposing flippase may be required to restore and maintain lipid asymmetry. Here, we identify the P4-ATPase ATP8B1 and its chaperone TMEM30B as selectively expressed in mouse outer hair cells (OHCs), enriched in stereocilia, and upregulated following the onset of MET and hearing. Loss of either protein results in elevated auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds, phosphatidylserine (PS) externalization, and rapid hair-cell degeneration, demonstrating that lipid homeostasis is crucial for OHC survival. Together, these findings establish ATP8B1 and TMEM30B as key regulators of membrane lipid asymmetry in sensory hair cells and establish TMEM30B as a novel deafness gene.

eLife.title: Pre-rRNA represses gene transcription in the XY body of male germ cells
eLife.abstract: Nucleolus is disassembled when the nuclear envelope breaks down during mitosis prophase. However, the dynamics of nucleolus in meiotic prophase remain unclear. Here, by tracking nucleolar components of spermatocytes in mice, we show that the nucleolus is fragmented even before the breakdown of the nuclear envelope. Instead of dissolving in nucleoplasm or cytoplasm, the nucleolar components are reaggregated and fused with the XY body during prophase I of meiosis. The dynamic relocation of the nucleolar components to the XY body is governed by the ATR-dependent signaling pathway. Moreover, the relocated pre-ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) covers the entire X and Y chromosomes. The treatment with RNA polymerase I inhibitor BMH-21 only disrupts the accumulation of pre-rRNA but not other nucleolar components on the X and Y chromosomes. Surprisingly, this disruption of pre-rRNA induces the recruitment of RNA polymerase II to the XY body and partially abolishes meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI). Taken together, this study reveals pre-rRNA as a key epigenetic regulator for MSCI.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Correction to 'Multiplexed CRISPR base editing enables pulse-activated irreversible biocontainment of engineered bacteria'.
Rapid degradation of six class I HDAC complexes reveals a mixture of unique, cooperative, and antagonistic roles.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The class I histone deacetylases (HDACs) 1, 2, and 3 form seven families of distinct large multiprotein complexes that regulate gene expression via deacetylation of lysines in histone tails. The degree of redundancy and functional overlap between complexes and their acute gene targets remain unknown. We used CRISPR/Cas9 to create six cell lines in which individual HDAC complexes were tagged with FKBP12F36V enabling rapid (<1 h), PROTAC-mediated, degradation. RNA sequencing at 6 h reveals that together, the four major complexes (CoREST, NuRD, NCoR/SMRT, and SIN3A) perturbed >50% of expressed genes. More than 60% of these are regulated by a single complex. ChIP-sequencing revealed that >54% of differentially expressed genes are directly regulated by the associated complex. Of genes regulated by more than one complex, approaching 50% are reciprocally regulated such that HDAC complexes act as antagonistic regulators. Homer analysis strongly suggests that the complexes are reliant on different transcription factors. This is the first study to rapidly degrade individual HDAC complexes, and identify and compare their acute gene targets. Together, these results show HDAC complexes regulate specific gene sets with minimal overlap of gene regulation within the same biological system.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Translons upstream of protein-coding regions rather than their products are crucial for proliferation of human cells of distinct origin.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are a widespread class of translated regions (translons) occurring in 5' leaders of messenger RNAs. They serve critical roles in post-transcriptional regulation and some are known to encode small proteins and peptideins. Yet it is not known which of these modes of function is more critical for human cells. We conducted a CRISPR-Cas9 mutagenesis screening targeting 969 translated human uORFs across three cell lines of distinct origin. Disruption of 155 uORFs impaired cell proliferation, although these effects were highly cell-type specific, with only six shared across all cell lines. Neither evolutionary conservation, comparative protein-coding potential, nor population mutational constraint distinguished uORF hits. Instead, high-throughput analysis of CRISPR-induced mutations combined with reporter assays demonstrated that proliferation phenotypes arise from altered cis-regulation of coding sequence (CDS) translation. In particular, uORFs located within short 5' leaders were disproportionately sensitive to indels, which frequently changed the uORF-CDS configuration, resulting in altered gene expression. We further identified naturally occurring human variants that are predicted to perturb these uORFs-CDS configurations, potentially contributing to disease phenotypes. Together, these findings identify uORF translation as a pervasive layer of gene-expression control. This study demonstrates that for most uORFs, it is their native translation rather than the activity of their products that is critical for the proliferation of human cells. It also provides a systematic resource for investigating uORF functions.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: AAV-mediated XIST deletion in female human hepatocytes with skewed X-inactivation induces limited reactivation of the X-linked OTC gene in vivo.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Reactivation of silenced wild-type alleles on the inactive X chromosome (Xi) offers a promising therapeutic avenue for X-linked disorders affecting females. The long non-coding RNA XIST is central to Xi silencing, yet its complete loss risks chromosome-wide dosage imbalance. To explore reactivation in a translational context, we employed chimeric mouse-human FRG livers repopulated with primary hepatocytes from a female patient with ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency exhibiting highly skewed X-inactivation. Adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated CRISPR-Cas9 delivery was used to disrupt XIST in vivo to assess effects on chromatin landscape and OTC expression. Despite differential XIST promoter methylation, the Xi remained accessible to CRISPR-Cas9, with editing frequencies comparable to those of the active X chromosome. XIST deletion induced limited reactivation of the wild-type OTC allele and was accompanied by broader epigenetic effects. CUT&RUN profiling distinguished effects of vector delivery and XIST deletion, including global H3K4me3 reduction after AAV transduction, X chromosome-restricted H3K27me3 reduction after XIST deletion, and broader H3K27ac reduction in edited hepatocytes. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of manipulating the human Xi in vivo while revealing distinct Xi-specific and broader chromatin effects. Together, they highlight the need for precise, locus-specific strategies to achieve therapeutic gene reactivation while preserving chromosome-wide epigenetic regulation.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Endogenous variability in transcription factor concentrations shapes their genome-wide occupancy.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The control of transcription factor (TF) concentrations is crucial for the precise regulation of gene expression and cell fate decisions during development. Yet, TF concentrations can display substantial temporal fluctuations and intercellular variations. How TF levels quantitatively shape genome-wide occupancy patterns remains largely unexplored. Here, we systematically investigate how physiological fluctuations in the concentrations of the pluripotency TFs OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG impact their genomic binding profiles in mouse embryonic stem cells. We uncover distinct concentration-dependent binding behaviors for each TF. NANOG occupancy increased monotonously with its concentration, even though a common set of regions made accessible by OCT4 and SOX2 are highly and uniformly bound at all NANOG concentrations. In contrast, SOX2 occupancy does not increase with its concentrations, while OCT4 displayed an intermediate behavior. Our results challenge the notion that TF binding follows simple mass-action dynamics and reveal a core set of pluripotency regions that are bound by all three TFs at all TF concentrations, revealing how pluripotency can be maintained despite marked fluctuations in core pluripotency TFs.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Reprogramming mRNA localization by targeted RNA-protein interference reveals roles in oncogenesis.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) associate with RNAs in intricate ribonucleoprotein complexes and regulate various aspects of RNA life cycle and, by extension, cell functions. Despite their significance, elucidating the functional contributions of specific RNA-RBP binding events, particularly in long-term phenotypic assays, remains challenging. Here, we harness the specificity of CRISPR/dCas13 to interfere with specific RNA-RBP interactions. We apply this methodology to GA-rich mRNA localization elements which recruit the RNA-binding protein CNBP and serve as platforms for the assembly of mRNA trafficking complexes. We show that dCas13/gRNA binds to target transcripts in a highly specific manner and interferes with CNBP recruitment leading to altered target mRNA localization and cell motility, consistent with the function of the targeted mRNAs. We describe optimizations and considerations for the stable implementation of this system. We further use it to show that interfering with the localization of the GA-containing NET1 mRNA reduces cancer cell invasiveness and metastatic lung colonization. These data reveal a potential role for mRNA localization in oncogenic progression and illustrate how this CRISPR-based system can be used for long-term functional investigations of RNA-RBP interactions in vivo.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: MissenseDB: proteome-wide human missense variant effect prediction database with structural context.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Missense variant-effect predictors now provide proteome-scale estimates of amino acid substitution impact, but their outputs remain distributed across independent resources and are difficult to explore jointly with protein structural and human-variation context. We present MissenseDB, a residue-centric database integrating three architecturally distinct transformer-based predictors, AlphaMissense, VESM-3B, and VESPA, across the reviewed human proteome. MissenseDB contains 10 734 339 residue positions across 19 436 canonical human proteins, with complete three-predictor coverage for 19 434 proteins. Predictor outputs are linked to 211 731 UniProt-to-structure mappings, residue-level secondary-structure and molecular-context annotations, and Pfam domain membership, together with 59 851 HUMSAVAR missense variants enriched with population allele frequencies and ClinVar annotations. Raw predictor scores are provided together with empirically calibrated probabilities referenced to a common prior, on which a single decision threshold applies; on this calibrated scale all three predictors agree on ~75%-77% of pathogenic and benign variants. An interactive interface couples protein-wide sequence tracks with three-dimensional structural visualization and provides access to the complete 19-substitution landscape at individual residues. REST endpoints support protein-, residue-, and proteome-scale retrieval, while versioned relational database snapshots and a genomic coordinate lookup table enabling direct mapping from GRCh38 VCF coordinates to UniProt residues enable reproducible bulk analysis. MissenseDB is freely accessible without registration at https://biosig.lab.uq.edu.au/missense_db.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: BGC Atlas v2: biosynthetic gene clusters with taxonomic and environmental context at scale.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Genomic and metagenomic studies have revealed that microbes have the capacity to produce an enormous diversity of secondary metabolites. These compounds play important roles in microbial interactions and are also a major source of medicines and other useful natural products, yet only a small fraction of this biosynthetic potential has been experimentally characterized. BGC Atlas was developed to explore this largely uncharacterized diversity by placing biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into genomic and environmental context. Here, we present BGC Atlas v2, which expands the collection more than eight-fold to >16 million predicted BGCs and extends it from metagenomic assemblies to metagenome-assembled genomes, single-amplified genomes, and isolate genomes. The new release provides taxonomic assignments for nearly all BGCs, harmonized environmental metadata, nested searches across biosynthetic, taxonomic, environmental and geographic properties, and protein-sequence searches against BGC-encoded genes. Its scale also reveals how much bacterial and archaeal biosynthetic diversity remains unexplored. By connecting pathways to related families, organisms, and environments, BGC Atlas v2 supports natural-product discovery and investigations of prokaryotic biosynthetic diversity across taxa and ecosystems. BGC Atlas v2 is freely available at https://bgc-atlas.ziemertlab.com/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: BFVD v3-the atlas of predicted viral protein structures.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The Big Fantastic Virus Database (BFVD) v3 is the most comprehensive resource for ColabFold-AlphaFold2-predicted viral protein structures. It holds 5 776 417 structures of nearly all viral sequences in UniProt 2025_03, a 16.4-fold increase compared to the representative-only catalogs of BFVD v1 and v2. Structure prediction quality has also improved, with high-confidence predictions accounting for 75.3% of BFVD v3 entries. Contributing factors include Logan's enormous sequence assembly, now mined for the entire BFVD v3 instead of only for shallow alignments, alongside continued prediction quality improvements. BFVD v3 covers 72.7% of International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses virus species, 1.54-fold more than BFVD v2. With this version, the fraction of fully covered viral reference proteomes increases from 1.5% to 72.6%. BFVD v3 thus brings us closer to a structural catalog of the known virosphere and is freely available at bfvd.steineggerlab.workers.dev and bfvd.foldseek.com.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: VEuPathDB: 2026 update on data, tools, and infrastructure for eukaryotic pathogens, vectors, and hosts.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The eukaryotic pathogen, vector, and host informatics resource (VEuPathDB, https://veupathdb.org) provides open access to genomic and other large-scale data for protozoan and fungal pathogens, arthropod vectors, and their hosts, supporting >800 organisms and 2602 datasets across 12 component databases, OrthoMCL, and the newly added dataExplorer, as of Release 71 (August 2026). Since our last update, 292 datasets have been integrated, gene product descriptions improved, and OrthoMCL expanded to over 819 000 orthology groups spanning 9.2 million proteins. Artificial intelligence-assisted approaches now support dataset curation, community gene annotation, and experimental summaries of transcriptomic evidence on gene pages, each subject to expert or user review. The new My Datasets workspace lets researchers upload, analyze, and share their own data alongside curated datasets, and a guided interface supports differential expression analysis without programming. Infrastructure has been consolidated from 15 Oracle databases into a single PostgreSQL platform, with data-processing pipelines migrated to containerized Nextflow workflows. This period was also defined by the loss of the long-standing US federal award that funded VEuPathDB, its temporary closure in September 2024, and its restoration under a community-supported model of voluntary tiered subscriptions, donations, and philanthropic support, with all data and tools remaining freely accessible.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: miRTarBase 11.0: an evidence-centred resource for experimentally supported microRNA-target interactions.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression through sequence-dependent interactions with target RNAs, but different experimental approaches capture distinct aspects of miRNA-target interactions (MTIs). miRTarBase 11.0 contains 9771 947 MTI records derived from literature curation, integrated CLASHub chimeric-pairing data and processed Argonaute cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (AGO-CLIP) data, encompassing 5010 miRNAs and 31 539 target genes. To support interaction-level interpretation, the resource distinguishes direct pairing evidence, AGO occupancy, functional validation, and contextual support. Integration of CLASHub provides binding-site-resolved evidence of direct miRNA-target pairing, while updated AGO CLIP processing defines high-confidence and conserved interaction classes. A rule-based score summarises annotated targeting or binding methods, protein- and RNA-related assays, rescue experiments, and functional assays, while complementary tiers distinguish method combinations. RNA2Immune places MTIs in immune-cell and disease contexts; Rfam 15.0 and miRBase v23 provide harmonized miRNA family, sequence, and identifier annotations; and NPInter v5.0 links upstream noncoding RNA regulators to miRNA-target networks. A Qwen3.6-27B-assisted workflow supports full-text and figure-based curation with human verification. The redesigned Django and Nginx platform supports secure operation, stable deployment and responsive access to evidence-ranked searches, contextual browsing, network views, and data downloads. miRTarBase 11.0 is freely available without registration at https://awi.cuhk.edu.cn/miRTarBase/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: MIsoTEx: a mammalian transcript-isoform classification framework and database for exploring tissue distribution, expression stability, and abundance patterns.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Alternative splicing generates transcript isoforms with distinct tissue-expression patterns, but resources integrating transcript distribution, abundance consistency, and relative abundance remain limited. We developed MIsoTEx (Mammalian Isoform Tissue Expression Resource), a database and expression-pattern-based classification framework for protein-coding iso-mRNAs in human, mouse, and rat. RNA-seq datasets from GTEx, ARCHS4, and newly curated datasets from SRA were used to construct catalogs, following stringent selection of normal adult tissue samples. Ubiquitously detected iso-mRNAs were classified as uniformly abundant (UUni) or variably abundant (UVar), while tissue-associated iso-mRNAs were classified as tissue-predominant (TPred), tissue-exclusive (TExcl), tissue-poor (TPoor), or tissue-absent (TAbsn). These classes were further divided into five relative-abundance sub-classes, with confidence scores assigned to tissue-associated classifications. MIsoTEx contains ~147 000 protein-coding iso-mRNAs and supports gene- and transcript-based queries, tissue-pattern searches, cross-species comparison of orthologs with concordant expression, and analysis of user-supplied expression data to identify candidate control iso-mRNAs. Comparisons with independent RNA-seq, RT-PCR, and published expression datasets provided support for aspects of the classification framework. Functional enrichment analysis revealed distinct biological associations among selected expression-based categories. MIsoTEx facilitates transcript-level exploration of mammalian tissue-expression patterns and helps identify candidate reference iso-mRNAs for experimental evaluation. The database can be accessed using the link: https://resources.ibab.ac.in/MIsoTEx/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: Conserved Domain Database 2026 update.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Protein domain and protein family models comprising the Conserved Domain Database (CDD) are widely used at the National Center of Biotechnology Information to inform protein textual and graphical summary pages with the location of domain footprints, domain architecture, and derived functional sites, and to name proteins by domain architecture when names cannot be obtained from higher-ranked, more specific sources. CDD continues to add novel protein domain models, constructed as multiple sequence alignments, to its collection via import of external data sources and an in-house curation effort. CDD has been available publicly for ~25 years and continues to update a substantial archive of pre-computed annotation for rapid dissemination of information, provide live database search services that can support moderate numbers of requests, and downloadable data and software to run data analyses locally. CDD can be accessed at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Structure/cdd/cdd.shtml.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: MGnify analyses in 2027: enhancing the depth and breadth of analyses across metabarcoding, unassembled metagenomes, and assembled datasets.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Microbiome derived nucleic acid sequence analysis has become an increasingly important aspect of many scientific fields. MGnify (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/metagenomics/) provides standardized, versioned analysis pipelines for the taxonomic and functional characterization of microbiome samples. The latest release of the MGnify pipelines (version 6) provides amplicon sequence variant analysis, expanded functional annotations including viral and mobilome for assembly analysis, and a streamlined minimal raw-reads analysis. We have improved the reusability of the pipelines through transition to Nextflow as a workflow language and have undertaken a substantial overhaul of our automation systems, using Prefect to orchestrate the pipeline execution. Finally, we have released a new version of our programmatic and bulk access services to better support large-scale computational access of data, as well as rationalizing our contig browser to improve in-browser performance. These improvements serve to support the use of MGnify pipelines and data products going forward, and improve the AI-readiness of our outputs.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: DrugMAP 3.0: an enriched molecular atlas featuring ADMET endpoints, pharmacogenomic perturbations, and bioactivity atlas of drugs.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: The paradigm of targeted therapeutics has shifted from static drug-target interactions to systemic absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) endpoints, dynamic transcriptomic perturbation signatures, and quantitative binding affinities, thereby amplifying the demand for multidimensional pharmacological atlases. In other words, it is necessary to bridge systemic safety profiles, cellular responses, and molecular interactions. However, such integrative data were inadequately covered by existing databases. In this study, DrugMAP was therefore substantially updated, which accumulated (i) 112 470 fine-grained ADMET endpoint profiles covering 126 endpoints for over 7680 drugs; (ii) 406 360 pharmacogenomic signatures for 3484 chemical perturbations and 11 033 molecules; and (iii) a quantitative bioactivity atlas covering molecular affinities, cellular sensitivity, and cytotoxicity for over 15 812 drugs and 4155 drug-interacting molecules. With the growing demand for quantitative pharmacology and the rapidly growing interest in AI-assisted drug discovery, DrugMAP is expected to act as an indispensable supplement to existing databases to facilitate drug discovery. DrugMAP is freely accessible at https://idrblab.org/drugmap/.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: PhageScope 2.0: a million-scale resource for integrated exploration of phage genomic, functional, and structural diversity.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Understanding phage diversity is essential for studying microbial ecosystems and developing phage-based applications. However, existing phage databases lack systematic integration of protein family and structural information. Here, we present PhageScope 2.0 (https://phagescope.deepomics.org), a database and analysis platform for exploring phage genomic, functional, and structural diversity. The update incorporates 12 environmental and metagenomic data sources, expanding the collection to 2 576 925 phage sequences, with 12 610 425 protein families and structures for 58 314 540 proteins. The platform supports family-based exploration of functional annotations and genomic neighbourhoods, structure visualization, structure search with Foldseek, and sequence-based structure-similarity prediction with TM-Vec. New and updated tools further support phage recovery from sequencing reads and cross-checking of host, lifestyle, and taxonomic predictions against existing annotations. Together, these updates enable integrated exploration of phage diversity and guide functional studies of poorly characterized proteins.

Nucleic Acids Research.title: CellColocDB: a disease-centred resource linking GWAS loci to genes, cell contexts, and fine-mapping evidence.
Nucleic Acids Research.abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified disease-associated loci, but linking these signals to molecular mechanisms remains difficult because of linkage disequilibrium and context-dependent genetic regulation. CellColocDB is a disease- and window-centred resource integrating GWAS-QTL colocalization across bulk, sorted-cell, and single-cell QTL datasets. The current release includes 2805 GWAS datasets covering 1201 diseases and traits and 40 516 GWAS windows, together with 23 QTL sources, 316 QTL contexts, and 89 842 molecular features. CellColocDB contains 3 572 118 coloc.abf results with PP.H4 > 0.5, including 1 609 418 with PP.H4 ≥ 0.8. Analyses are organized as GWAS dataset × GWAS window × QTL context × molecular feature tasks, allowing contexts and molecular features to be compared within the same GWAS region. coloc.abf is the primary colocalization analysis, with coloc-SuSiE and SMR/HEIDI providing complementary evidence where available. Task-specific ABF top SNPs are linked to CAUSALdb2 fine-mapping results from seven methods. Results are available through disease-, QTL context-, gene-, and locus-level views, with regional association tracks and matched variants, and can be queried by gene, genomic region, or GWAS window ID. CellColocDB is freely available at http://www.mulinlab.org/colocdb/.
